anatomy.articles: [RTL] Articles on heart anatomy and function
anatomy.intro: [RTL] A 3D model of a normal adult heart. Rotate it, pick a structure from the list or click it on the model, make the chambers see-through or cut the heart open to look inside.
anatomy.title: [RTL] Heart anatomy
congenital.signsNote: [RTL] The features are named as in the sources of the article; they are not marked on the model.
congenital.source: [RTL] Model record in the NIH 3D Heart Library
congenital.tetralogy-of-fallot.caption: [RTL] The heart of a patient with tetralogy of Fallot, a model built from MRI scans in the NIH 3D Heart Library. It is one person's heart: in other patients the shape and size differ. NIH did not take part in Heart Atlas and does not endorse it.
congenital.tetralogy-of-fallot.posterAlt: [RTL] The heart of a patient with tetralogy of Fallot, cut from the front: heart muscle and the blood inside the chambers and vessels
congenital.tetralogy-of-fallot.sign2: [RTL] Right ventricular outflow tract obstruction and pulmonary valve stenosis
congenital.tetralogy-of-fallot.signs: [RTL] Four features of tetralogy of Fallot
congenital.transposition-of-the-great-ar: [RTL] The heart of a child with transposition of the great arteries before surgery: a model of the blood in the chambers and vessels from the NIH 3D Heart Library. Blue is the blood of the systemic circulation (venae cavae, right atrium and ventricle, aorta), red the blood of the pulmonary circulation (pulmonary veins, left atrium and ventricle, pulmonary artery). The model is enlarged. It is one person's heart: in other patients the shape and size differ. NIH did not take part in Heart Atlas and does not endorse it.

[RTL] The heart of a child with transposition of the great arteries, from the front: the blue systemic circulation with the aorta rising from the right ventricle, and the red pulmonary circulation behind it
[RTL] Ventriculo-arterial discordance: the aorta originates from the right ventricle, the pulmonary artery from the left ventricle
[RTL] Independent, parallel pulmonary and systemic circulations
[RTL] Two features of transposition of the great arteries
diagram.abdominal-aortic-aneurysm.title: [RTL] Diagram of the abdominal aorta with the renal and iliac arteries: normally the aorta below the renal arteries is on average 18–22 mm across; in an abdominal aortic aneurysm this segment usually widens all round to 3 cm or more, and a blood clot often lines its wall from inside
diagram.acute-limb-ischemia.title: [RTL] Diagram of the main artery of the leg, which divides into the lower leg arteries below the knee: normally blood flows through them to the foot and there is a pulse on the foot; in acute limb ischaemia an embolus is stuck where the artery branches, there is no blood flow below it, no pulse on the foot, and the foot is pale and cold
diagram.aortic-dissection.title: [RTL] Diagram of the aorta cut lengthwise: normally the three-layer wall is intact and blood flows in one lumen; in aortic dissection blood passes through an intimal tear into the middle layer of the wall, and a flap of intima separates the true lumen from the false lumen
diagram.aortic-regurgitation.title: [RTL] Diagram of the left heart in diastole, while the left ventricle fills from the left atrium: normally the aortic valve leaflets are closed; in aortic regurgitation they do not close and blood flows back from the aorta into the left ventricle
diagram.aortic-stenosis.title: [RTL] Diagram of the aortic valve: normally, in aortic stenosis and after the valve is replaced with a prosthesis
diagram.arrhythmogenic-right-ventricular: [RTL] Diagram of the right and left ventricles in section and of the right ventricular wall tissue: normally the right ventricular wall is heart muscle whose cells are held together by desmosomes; in late-stage arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy the right ventricle is dilated, its wall is thinner, and in the outflow part, the inflow part and at the apex the muscle is replaced by fatty and fibrous tissue
diagram.atrial-fibrillation.title: [RTL] Diagram of the electrical impulse in the heart in normal sinus rhythm and in atrial fibrillation
diagram.atrial-flutter.title: [RTL] Diagram of the atria and ventricles: normally the impulse from the sinus node spreads over the atria and passes through the AV node to the ventricles; in typical atrial flutter the impulse runs in a large circle in the right atrium around the ring of the tricuspid valve, counterclockwise, through the isthmus between the inferior vena cava and the valve, and usually every second impulse reaches the ventricles
diagram.atrial-septal-defect.title: [RTL] Diagram of the heart chambers: normal, with an atrial septal defect and after the defect is closed
diagram.atrioventricular-septal-defect.t: [RTL] Diagram of the four heart chambers normally and in the complete form of atrioventricular septal defect: normally the right and left halves of the heart are separate and blood flows from the atria into the ventricles through two separate valves, the tricuspid and the mitral; in the complete form there is one large defect in the centre of the heart directly above and below a common valve through which both atria connect with the ventricles, blood shunts from left to right at the atrial and the ventricular level, and all four chambers are enlarged
diagram.av-block.title: [RTL] Diagram of impulses travelling from the sinus node through the atria and the atrioventricular node to the ventricles: normally every impulse gets through; in second-degree atrioventricular block one impulse is blocked and the ventricles skip a beat
diagram.bicuspid-aortic-valve.title: [RTL] Diagram of the closed aortic valve seen from the aorta: normally the valve has three cusps that meet in the centre; a bicuspid aortic valve has two cusps, a smaller one and a larger one formed by two fused cusps, which carries a fusion line; the valve is not drawn narrowed
diagram.blood-flow.title: [RTL] Diagram of blood flow through the heart, lungs and body
diagram.brugada-syndrome.title: [RTL] ECG diagram of the right precordial leads V1 and V2: normally the ST segment after the QRS complex runs along the baseline; in the type 1 Brugada pattern the J point and the ST segment are raised, and the coved ST segment descends into an inverted T wave
diagram.cardiac-amyloidosis.title: [RTL] Diagram of the heart cut through all four chambers while the ventricles fill: normally the ventricular walls are of normal thickness and the valves and the septum between the atria are thin; in cardiac amyloidosis there are amyloid deposits in the walls; the walls of both ventricles, the valves and the septum between the atria are thickened, there is a little fluid in the pericardium and the left atrium is enlarged
diagram.cardiac-myxoma.title: [RTL] Diagram of the heart cut through all four chambers while the ventricles fill: normally the mitral valve is open and blood flows freely from the left atrium into the left ventricle; with a myxoma a rounded lobular tumour hangs in the left atrium on a stalk attached to the interatrial septum, swings with the blood flow, drops into the opening of the mitral valve and obstructs blood flow into the left ventricle
diagram.cardiac-sarcoidosis.title: [RTL] Diagram of a four-chamber section of the heart with the conduction system: normally the impulse from the sinus node travels over the atria, through the atrioventricular node, the bundle of His and its branches to the ventricles; in cardiac sarcoidosis there are foci (granulomas) in the heart muscle (their places in the diagram are an example): in the interventricular septum at the bundle of His, where the impulse stops, and in the walls of the left and right ventricles
diagram.cardiac-tamponade.title: [RTL] Diagram of the heart cut through all four chambers inside the pericardium while the ventricles fill: normally a thin layer of fluid lies between the layers of the pericardium and the chambers fill freely; in cardiac tamponade a layer of fluid or blood surrounds the heart, which is not enlarged, and presses on it, the right atrium and right ventricle are compressed, and all chambers are smaller because they fill less
diagram.catecholaminergic-polymorphic-ve: [RTL] Diagram of the electrical impulse path from the sinus node through the atria and the AV node to the ventricles, with a ventricular cell close up: at rest the impulse takes its usual route, the rhythm is regular and the calcium stays in the cell's internal store; during exertion or emotion stress hormones reach the heart, the store leaks extra calcium and extra impulses start from several points in the ventricles, while the structure of the heart does not change
diagram.chronic-thromboembolic-pulmonary: [RTL] Diagram of the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery with its branches in the lung: normally all branches are open and the right ventricle is of normal size; in chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension organised fibrotic material narrows some branches with a ring-like narrowing or a web and blocks one branch completely, less blood reaches the lung beyond it, the open branches are overfilled, and the right ventricle has a thickened wall and a dilated cavity
diagram.coarctation-of-the-aorta.title: [RTL] Diagram of the left ventricle, the aortic arch with its branches to the head and arms, and the descending aorta: normally, in coarctation of the aorta and after it is repaired. In coarctation there is a narrowing just past the left subclavian artery, high pressure above the narrowing, less blood flow below it and a thickened left ventricular wall; after repair blood flows freely down the aorta again
diagram.conduction-system.title: [RTL] Diagram of the conduction system: the impulse from the sinoatrial node to the Purkinje fibres
diagram.congenitally-corrected-transposi: [RTL] Diagram of the circulation, normally and in congenitally corrected transposition of the great arteries: normally the right atrium connects through the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle and the left atrium through the mitral valve to the left ventricle; in corrected transposition the ventricles have swapped places together with their valves, yet venous blood still goes to the lungs and arterial blood to the body; the right ventricle pumps blood into the aorta, which lies in front and to the left, and blood often leaks back through the tricuspid valve into the left atrium
diagram.constrictive-pericarditis.title: [RTL] Diagram of the heart cut through all four chambers inside the pericardium while the ventricles fill: normally the pericardium is thin with a narrow cavity under it and the chambers fill freely; in constrictive pericarditis the pericardium is thick and stiff with patches of calcium and no wide layer of fluid under it, the atria are enlarged, and the ventricles are of normal size but fill less
diagram.coronary-arteries.title: [RTL] Diagram of the coronary arteries, front view of the heart
diagram.coronary-heart-disease.title: [RTL] Diagram of a coronary artery supplying the heart muscle: normal, and narrowed by plaques with one branch blocked by a blood clot
diagram.deep-vein-thrombosis.title: [RTL] Diagram of part of the lower leg with a deep vein in longitudinal section: normally blood flows up the vein towards the heart through open valves; in deep vein thrombosis a clot starts at a valve and grows up the vein, blood flow below it is slowed, the leg below the clot swells, and a piece of the clot can break off and travel to the lungs (pulmonary embolism)
diagram.dilated-cardiomyopathy.title: [RTL] Diagram of the size of the left ventricle and how much it contracts, normally and in dilated cardiomyopathy
diagram.dyslipidemia.title: [RTL] Diagram of an artery cut lengthwise: normally LDL particles pass along the lumen with the blood; with high LDL cholesterol there are more of them, they are retained in the wall and form an early plaque
diagram.ebstein-anomaly.title: [RTL] Diagram of the right heart: normally the tricuspid valve leaflets attach to the annulus between the right atrium and the right ventricle; in Ebstein anomaly the anterior leaflet is enlarged and sail-like, the septal leaflet is stuck to the septum and displaced towards the apex, the part of the ventricle between the annulus and the leaflets is atrialised, the functional ventricle is smaller, blood flows back through the valve, and the right atrium is drawn larger
diagram.eisenmenger-syndrome.title: [RTL] Diagram of the ventricles, the pulmonary artery, the aorta and small lung arteries in cross-section: normally the septum between the ventricles is intact, there is no shunt, and the walls of the small lung arteries are thin; in Eisenmenger syndrome there is a large defect in the septum, the pressure in the pulmonary artery is high, the walls of the small lung arteries are thickened, blood crosses the defect from right to left, and mixed blood enters the aorta
diagram.extrasystole.title: [RTL] Diagram of the electrical impulse path from the sinus node through the atria to the ventricles, with an ECG strip: normally every beat starts in the sinus node and every QRS complex has a P wave before it; in a ventricular premature beat an extra impulse starts early in a focus in a ventricle, and on the ECG it is an early, wide QRS complex without a P wave, followed by a pause
diagram.fabry-disease.title: [RTL] Diagram of a small area of the left ventricular wall seen close up, outer surface at the top and cavity at the bottom: normally the wall has its usual thickness and nothing builds up in the lysosomes of the muscle cells; in Fabry disease the wall is thicker, the muscle cells are larger, small deposits lie inside their lysosomes, and there are patches of fibrous tissue between the cells
diagram.familial-hypercholesterolemia.ti: [RTL] Diagram of a liver cell with blood above it: normally LDL receptors on the cell surface take up LDL particles and carry them into the cell, and there are few particles in the blood; in familial hypercholesterolaemia the receptors do not work or work less well, the cell takes up fewer particles, and many LDL particles stay in the blood
diagram.heart-chambers.title: [RTL] Diagram of the four heart chambers in diastole and systole
diagram.heart-failure.title: [RTL] Diagram of how strongly the ventricles contract and how much blood they eject, normally and in heart failure
diagram.heart-valves.title: [RTL] Diagram of the four heart valves in diastole and systole
diagram.holter-monitor.title: [RTL] Diagram of Holter monitoring: a recorder worn on the body and the ECG recording
diagram.hypertension.title: [RTL] Diagram of an artery and the left ventricle with normal and high blood pressure
diagram.hypertrophic-cardiomyopathy.titl: [RTL] Diagram of the left ventricle and its outflow into the aorta, normally and in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with a thickened septum
[RTL] Diagram of the circulation, normally and in hypoplastic left heart syndrome: normally blood passes through the lungs and the body in turn; in the defect the mitral and aortic valves are closed, the left ventricle is small, the ascending aorta and the aortic arch are narrow, blood from the left atrium crosses an atrial communication into the right atrium and mixes there with venous blood, and the right ventricle pumps the mixed blood into the pulmonary artery and through a patent ductus arteriosus into the aorta and on to the body
diagram.infective-endocarditis.title: [RTL] Diagram of a heart valve: normal, and in infective endocarditis with a vegetation, a damaged leaflet, backflow and a fragment breaking off
diagram.kawasaki-disease.title: [RTL] Diagram of the heart from the front with the coronary arteries: normally the artery wall does not bulge anywhere; in Kawasaki disease a coronary artery aneurysm may form, a part where the wall bulges out and the artery widens; as an example, the aneurysm is shown on the right coronary artery
diagram.label.aorta-anterior-left: [RTL] Aorta: in front and to the left
diagram.label.apex-mid-not-contracting: [RTL] Apex and mid walls do not contract
diagram.label.deep-vein-spread-risk: [RTL] Risk of the clot spreading into the deep vein
diagram.label.domed-valve: [RTL] Fused leaflets: a dome with a narrow opening
diagram.label.every-second-impulse: [RTL] Every second impulse: about 150 per minute
diagram.label.lv-pumps-to-aorta: [RTL] The LV pumps blood into the aorta
diagram.label.mitral-prolapse: [RTL] Leaflets bulge into the left atrium
diagram.label.much-blood-to-lungs: [RTL] Too much blood to the lungs
diagram.label.posterior-leaflet-prolapse: [RTL] Posterior leaflet bulges into the LA
diagram.label.rv-pumps-to-aorta: [RTL] The RV pumps blood into the aorta
diagram.label.to-abdomen-and-legs: [RTL] To the abdominal organs and legs
diagram.label.too-little-blood-to-brain: [RTL] Too little blood reaches the brain
diagram.label.ventricles-swapped: [RTL] The ventricles have swapped places with their valves
diagram.left-ventricular-noncompaction.t: [RTL] Diagram of a long-axis section of the left ventricle, base at the top and apex at the bottom: normally the wall is dense (compact), and its inner surface is shown smooth as a simplification; in left ventricular noncompaction the outer compact layer is thin, and inside it lies a thick spongy layer of trabeculae with deep recesses that open into the cavity, most marked at the apex; the ventricle is the same size
diagram.long-qt-syndrome.title: [RTL] ECG diagram: normally the QT interval runs from the start of the QRS complex to the end of the T wave; in long QT syndrome the T wave ends later and the QT interval is longer; below, a normal rhythm and torsades de pointes ventricular tachycardia, with complexes that change around the baseline
diagram.marfan-syndrome.title: [RTL] Diagram of the left heart and the aortic root while the left ventricle contracts: normally the mitral valve leaflets close; in Marfan syndrome the aortic root is widened, starting from the sinuses, and the mitral valve leaflets bulge back into the left atrium
diagram.mitral-regurgitation.title: [RTL] Diagram of the mitral valve while the left ventricle contracts: closed normally, and in mitral regurgitation with a gap between the leaflets and blood flowing back into the left atrium, drawn larger as in severe regurgitation
diagram.mitral-stenosis.title: [RTL] Diagram of the mitral valve while the left ventricle fills (diastole): normally the leaflets open wide and blood flows freely from the left atrium into the ventricle; in rheumatic mitral stenosis the leaflets are thickened and fused into a funnel with a narrow opening, and the left atrium is enlarged
diagram.mitral-valve-prolapse.title: [RTL] Lengthwise diagram of the left heart while the left ventricle contracts: normally the mitral valve leaflets meet at the level of the valve annulus; in mitral valve prolapse the posterior leaflet is larger and bulges above the annulus line into the left atrium, and its chordae are longer and thinner; a dashed jet shows that the valve sometimes lets blood flow back into the atrium
diagram.myocardial-infarction.title: [RTL] Diagram of the left ventricle in longitudinal section and the artery that runs along its inferior wall: normally blood flows through the right coronary artery to the muscle of the inferior wall; in ST-elevation myocardial infarction a clot on a plaque closes the artery completely, blood goes no further, and the part of the inferior wall beyond the blockage dies through the full thickness of the wall
diagram.myocarditis.title: [RTL] Diagram of a cross-section of the left ventricle: a uniform wall normally, and patchy foci of inflammation in the wall in myocarditis
diagram.natriuretic-peptides.title: [RTL] Diagram: proBNP is cleaved into the active hormone BNP and the inactive fragment NT-proBNP
diagram.partial-anomalous-pulmonary-veno: [RTL] Diagram of the circulation, normally and in partial anomalous pulmonary venous return: normally the four pulmonary veins carry blood from the lungs into the left atrium; in the defect (one variant is shown) the right upper pulmonary vein drains into the superior vena cava close to where it joins the right atrium, there is a sinus venosus defect high in the septum between the atria, blood passes through it from left to right, the right atrium and right ventricle are enlarged, and the other three pulmonary veins drain into the left atrium as usual
diagram.patent-ductus-arteriosus.title: [RTL] Diagram of the aorta and pulmonary artery: normally, with a patent ductus arteriosus and after it is closed. Normally the duct has closed and become the ligamentum arteriosum; when it stays open, blood flows through it from the aorta into the pulmonary artery; after it is closed, blood no longer flows through it
diagram.pericarditis.title: [RTL] Diagram of the heart inside the pericardium: normal, and with inflamed pericardial layers and fluid between them
diagram.peripheral-artery-disease.title: [RTL] Diagram of the main artery of the leg from the femoral artery through the popliteal artery and the lower leg arteries to the foot: normally the lumen is open and blood reaches the foot freely; in lower extremity peripheral artery disease a plaque narrows the femoral–popliteal segment, less blood passes below the narrowing, thin collateral vessels run around it, and the calf is marked as the place of pain on walking
diagram.pulmonary-atresia-with-ventricul: [RTL] Diagram of the ventricles, pulmonary arteries and aorta, normally and in pulmonary atresia with ventricular septal defect (one of the variants): normally blood goes from the right ventricle into the pulmonary artery and through its branches to the lungs, and from the left ventricle into the aorta; with the defect, the right ventricular outflow ends blindly, the pulmonary arteries are thin, there is a large septal defect under the aorta, the aorta is shifted and sits over it, the right ventricular wall is thickened, blood from both ventricles mixes and goes into the aorta, and from there reaches the pulmonary arteries through the open arterial duct and collateral vessels from the aorta
diagram.pulmonary-embolism.title: [RTL] Diagram of venous blood flowing from a leg vein through the right side of the heart into the pulmonary artery branches: normal, and in pulmonary embolism with a clot in a leg vein and an embolus blocking one branch
diagram.pulmonary-hypertension.title: [RTL] Diagram of the right ventricle, the pulmonary artery and small lung arteries in cross-section: normally the small arteries have a thin wall and a wide lumen, and the mean pulmonary artery pressure is 20 mmHg or less; in pulmonary arterial hypertension the walls of the small arteries are thickened, the lumen is narrowed, the mean pulmonary artery pressure is above 20 mmHg, and the right ventricle has a thickened wall and a dilated cavity
diagram.pulmonary-valve-stenosis.title: [RTL] Diagram of the right ventricle, the pulmonary valve and the pulmonary trunk: normally the valve leaflets are thin and open wide, and blood flows freely from the right ventricle into the pulmonary artery; in typical valvular stenosis the leaflets are fused into a dome with a narrow opening, blood passes through it as a fast turbulent jet, the right ventricular wall is thickened and the pulmonary trunk beyond the valve is dilated
diagram.restrictive-cardiomyopathy.title: [RTL] Diagram of the four heart chambers while the ventricles fill: normally the elastic ventricular walls stretch and the ventricles fill easily with blood from the atria; in restrictive cardiomyopathy the stiff walls hardly stretch, the ventricles of normal size fill less well, and both atria are enlarged
diagram.rheumatic-heart-disease.title: [RTL] Diagram of the mitral valve seen from the left ventricle while it fills (diastole): normally the leaflets are thin, the commissures are free and the opening is wide; in rheumatic disease the leaflets are thickened, both commissures are fused and only a small oval opening remains; the heart chambers and blood flow are not shown
diagram.sick-sinus-syndrome.title: [RTL] Diagram of sinus node impulses travelling through the atria and the atrioventricular node to the ventricles: normally the sinus node fires regularly; in sick sinus syndrome two impulses in a row are missing and a pause follows; in the diagram neither the atria nor the ventricles are activated during the pause, and the beats from lower pacemakers that usually appear in a pause are not shown
diagram.single-ventricle.title: [RTL] Diagram of the circulation, normally and in single ventricle: normally the heart has four chambers and blood passes through the lungs and the body in turn; for the defect, one of its variants is shown, double-inlet left ventricle: both atria open into one large ventricle, the second ventricle remains a small outlet chamber joined to the main one by an opening, blood from the lungs and from the body mixes, and the mixed blood leaves into the pulmonary artery from the main ventricle and into the aorta from the outlet chamber
diagram.superficial-thrombophlebitis.tit: [RTL] Diagram of part of the leg in longitudinal section: a superficial vein in the fat under the skin and a deep vein in the muscle; near the top the superficial vein joins the deep vein (the junction). Normally blood flows up both veins towards the heart. In superficial thrombophlebitis a segment of the superficial vein is blocked by a blood clot and the fat and skin around it are inflamed; the deep vein is not affected, and a dashed arrow shows the risk of the clot spreading through the junction into the deep vein
diagram.supraventricular-tachycardia.tit: [RTL] Diagram of the electrical impulse path from the atria through the AV node to the ventricles: normally the impulse passes once, in one direction; in AV nodal re-entrant tachycardia an early impulse goes down the slow pathway, returns up the fast pathway and keeps circling, so the ventricles beat fast and regularly
diagram.takayasu-arteritis.title: [RTL] Diagram of the aortic arch and its three branches, front view: normally the origins of the branches are not narrowed and the pulse is normal in both arms; in Takayasu arteritis the wall of the aorta and of the branch origins is thickened, and the branch origins may narrow or close; as an example, the origin of the brachiocephalic trunk is shown narrowed and the origin of the left subclavian artery blocked, so less blood reaches the arms and the pulse in them is weak or absent
diagram.takotsubo-syndrome.title: [RTL] Diagram of the left ventricle in a long-axis view, base at the top and apex at the bottom; the solid outline is the ventricle before contraction, the dashed one at the end of contraction: normally all walls, the apex included, contract evenly and the cavity shrinks along its whole length; in takotsubo syndrome the base contracts strongly and forms a narrow neck, while the apex and mid walls do not contract, so the cavity stays round at the bottom, like an octopus trap
diagram.tetralogy-of-fallot.title: [RTL] Diagram of the ventricles, pulmonary artery and aorta, normally, in tetralogy of Fallot and after complete repair: in tetralogy, a ventricular septal defect, a narrowed right ventricular outflow tract, an aorta overriding the defect and a thickened right ventricular wall; after repair, the defect is closed with a patch, the right ventricular outflow is widened and blood may leak back from the pulmonary artery into the right ventricle
diagram.thoracic-aortic-aneurysm.title: [RTL] Diagram of the left ventricle and the thoracic aorta: the root, the ascending aorta, the arch with its branches and the descending thoracic aorta. Normally the aorta is not widened anywhere; in the example of a thoracic aortic aneurysm the tubular part of the ascending aorta above the root is widened, while the root and the rest of the aorta are of normal size
diagram.total-anomalous-pulmonary-venous: [RTL] Diagram of the circulation, normally and in total anomalous pulmonary venous return: normally the four pulmonary veins carry blood from the lungs into the left atrium; in the defect (the supracardiac type is shown) the pulmonary veins join a confluence behind the heart, the blood rises through a vertical vein into the superior vena cava and reaches the right atrium, mixes there with oxygen-poor blood and passes into the left side of the heart only through the opening between the atria, and the right atrium and right ventricle are enlarged
diagram.transposition-of-the-great-arter: [RTL] Diagram of the circulation, normally and in transposition of the great arteries: normally blood passes through the lungs and the body in turn; in transposition the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left, so each circuit loops back on itself, and a little blood mixes through an atrial communication and a patent ductus arteriosus
diagram.tricuspid-regurgitation.title: [RTL] Diagram of the right heart while the right ventricle contracts: normally the tricuspid valve leaflets are closed and blood leaves the ventricle into the pulmonary artery; in tricuspid regurgitation the leaflets do not close, some blood flows back into the right atrium, and the atrium is drawn larger
diagram.truncus-arteriosus.title: [RTL] Diagram of the ventricles and the vessels leaving them, normally and in truncus arteriosus (type I, one of the variants): normally the pulmonary artery leaves the right ventricle and divides into two branches, and the aorta leaves the left ventricle, each vessel with its own valve; with the defect, a single common trunk with one valve leaves the heart above a ventricular septal defect, both ventricles pump blood into it, a pulmonary artery leaves the trunk and divides into two branches, and mixed blood goes both to the body and to the lungs, with too much blood going to the lungs
diagram.varicose-veins.title: [RTL] Diagram of part of the leg in longitudinal section: a superficial vein under the skin, a deep vein in the muscle and a short connecting vein between them. Normally the superficial vein is narrow, the cusps of its valves meet, and blood flows up it towards the heart and through the connecting vein into the deep vein. In varicose veins the superficial vein is widened and twisted, the cusps of its valves do not meet, and blood flows back down it (reflux); the deep vein is unchanged
diagram.vasovagal-syncope.title: [RTL] Diagram of a standing person: normally blood pressure holds, the heart beats at its usual rhythm, blood returns through the leg veins to the heart, and the brain gets enough blood; in vasovagal syncope a trigger such as prolonged standing, pain or fear acts through the vagus nerve to widen the blood vessels and/or slow the heart rate, the leg veins are wider, blood pressure falls, less blood reaches the brain, and light-headedness and sometimes fainting follow
diagram.ventricular-fibrillation.title: [RTL] Diagram of the electrical impulse in the heart: normally the impulse from the sinus node goes through the atria and the AV node and spreads through the ventricles as one wave, so they contract and pump blood out; in ventricular fibrillation many small chaotic waves run in many places of the ventricles at once, the ventricles only quiver, and no blood is pumped out
diagram.ventricular-septal-defect.title: [RTL] Diagram of the heart chambers: normal, with a ventricular septal defect and after the defect is closed
diagram.ventricular-tachycardia.title: [RTL] Diagram of the electrical impulse path from the sinus node through the atria and the AV node to the ventricles: normally every beat starts in the sinus node; in ventricular tachycardia the impulse circles in the scar zone of the ventricular wall through a narrow isthmus, and every lap excites the ventricles again, so they beat fast and regularly on their own, apart from the atria
diagram.wpw-syndrome.title: [RTL] Diagram of the electrical impulse path from the sinus node through the atria to the ventricles, with the ECG of one beat: normally the impulse reaches the ventricles only through the AV node; in WPW syndrome an accessory pathway between an atrium and a ventricle conducts it earlier and excites part of the ventricle ahead of time, so on the ECG the PR interval is shorter, a delta wave appears at the start of the QRS complex and the QRS is wider

heartClock.ecgDescription: [RTL] Sinus rhythm at {rate} beats per minute. Each beat has a P wave, then a narrow QRS complex, then a T wave, and the intervals between beats are equal.
heartClock.ecgLabel: [RTL] Synthetic ECG, lead {lead}. Grid: 25 mm per second, 10 mm per millivolt.
heartClock.inModel: [RTL] How it looks in the model
heartClock.intro: [RTL] One timer drives the whole cardiac cycle. The ECG below is generated from it: change the heart rate and watch the waves and the phases of the cycle follow.
heartClock.preset.aortic-stenosis.ecg: [RTL] Sinus rhythm at {rate} beats per minute. Each beat has a P wave, then a narrow QRS complex, then a T wave, and the intervals between beats are equal.
heartClock.preset.aortic-stenosis.summar: [RTL] The aortic valve is narrowed: during ejection the pressure in the left ventricle is on average 40 mmHg higher than in the aorta, the threshold of severe stenosis. The model does not show the murmur, the slow-rising, weak pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus) or the softer second heart sound.
heartClock.preset.atrial-fibrillation.ec: [RTL] Atrial fibrillation at an average of {rate} beats per minute. There are no P waves, the baseline shows small irregular f waves, the QRS complexes are narrow, and the intervals between them differ.
heartClock.preset.atrial-fibrillation.su: [RTL] The atria fibrillate instead of contracting: there are no P waves, the baseline shows small irregular f waves, and the intervals between beats vary without a pattern. The atria no longer add the last part of ventricular filling.
heartClock.preset.atrial-flutter.ecg: [RTL] Atrial flutter at {rate} beats per minute. There are no P waves: the baseline is a regular sawtooth of F waves, two for every narrow QRS complex, and the intervals between beats are equal.
heartClock.preset.atrial-flutter.summary: [RTL] The atria are activated regularly at 250 to 350 per minute, and the ECG shows sawtooth F waves instead of P waves, with no flat line between them. The AV node lets every second impulse through to the ventricles (2:1 conduction), so the ventricles beat regularly at half the atrial rate. The model starts at 150 beats per minute, with F waves at 300 per minute, and keeps the ventricular rate from 126 to 175 so that the F waves stay in that range. The atria no longer add the last part of ventricular filling. The model does not show other conduction ratios (4:1, 3:1, or a varying ratio that makes the rhythm irregular), atypical flutter, or the F waves in other leads, such as the positive ones in V1.
heartClock.preset.atrial-premature-beats: [RTL] Sinus rhythm at {rate} beats per minute, and every fourth beat comes early. The early beat has a P wave and a usual narrow QRS complex. The next beat comes one usual interval after the early one, so the beats on either side of it are less than two usual intervals apart.

[RTL] A premature beat comes earlier than the next normal beat, from an impulse that starts outside the sinus node. In an atrial premature beat the impulse starts in the atria. It can reach the ventricles the normal way, with a narrow QRS, or be conducted abnormally or not at all; the model shows the normal way. It resets the sinus node, so the pause after it is shorter than a full compensatory pause. Here every fourth beat is premature, so that the premature beats are easy to see; that is a lot of them, not a typical picture. It comes at 0.7 of the usual interval, and the next beat comes one usual interval after it. These timings are model choices, since the sources give no numbers; the model draws the P wave of the premature beat with the same shape as the sinus one. The beat before the premature one is cut short, so the model also shortens its contraction; in a real heart the timings of a beat depend on the interval before it, not after it. In the model every beat pumps the same amount. The slider sets the sinus rate from 40 to 86; with this timing the model works only in that range. The model does not show premature beats at random times or in pairs, or where in the atria the impulse starts.
heartClock.preset.atrial-septal-defect.e: [RTL] Sinus rhythm at {rate} beats per minute. Each beat has a P wave, then a wide QRS complex, then a T wave, and the intervals between beats are equal.
heartClock.preset.atrial-septal-defect.s: [RTL] The second heart sound is split, and the split is the same on every beat. In atrial septal defect the ECG may show incomplete or complete right bundle branch block; the model only widens the QRS to the width of a complete block and does not draw its shape. Blood flows from the left atrium to the right, and the model shows only the left side of the heart, so the Wiggers diagram does not change. The model does not play the murmur.
[RTL] Sinus rhythm at {rate} beats per minute. Each beat has a P wave, then a long PR interval of more than 0.20 s, then a narrow QRS complex, then a T wave, and the intervals between beats are equal.

[RTL] The PR interval is longer than normal, more than 0.20 s. Every P wave is still followed by a QRS complex: every atrial impulse reaches the ventricles, only more slowly. This preset shows only first-degree block; second- and third-degree block, in which some or all atrial impulses do not reach the ventricles, have presets of their own.
heartClock.preset.av-block-second-degree: [RTL] Second-degree AV block, Mobitz I: P waves at a steady {rate} per minute. The PR interval grows with each beat until a P wave has no QRS complex after it; then the cycle starts again with the shortest PR. Three narrow QRS complexes for every four P waves.

[RTL] In second-degree AV block some impulses from the atria do not reach the ventricles: a P wave has no QRS complex after it. In Mobitz I (Wenckebach) the PR interval grows from beat to beat until a P wave is not conducted; the next beat has the shortest PR again, and the cycle repeats. Here the cycle has four P waves and three QRS complexes (4:3), and the QRS is narrow, as when the block is in the AV node. The slider sets the rate of the P waves; the ventricles beat at three quarters of it. A PR of 180 ms at 60 per minute, its equal growth of 80 ms per beat, the P wave rate of 60 to start with and the upper limit of 70 are model choices, since the sources give no numbers; because the growth is equal, the gaps between QRS complexes inside a cycle are equal too. Mobitz I often needs no treatment; a permanent pacemaker is recommended when the block causes clear symptoms and transient or reversible causes have been ruled out. The model does not show 2:1 or high-grade block, the atrial a wave after a P wave that is not conducted, or the atria contracting on the 3D model.

[RTL] Second-degree AV block, Mobitz II: P waves at a steady {rate} per minute with the same PR interval before every narrow QRS complex. Every third P wave has no QRS after it, and the gap between QRS complexes across it is twice the others.

[RTL] In Mobitz II second-degree AV block a P wave has no QRS complex after it, and the PR interval is the same before and after it. Usually every third or fourth P wave is not conducted; here every third, so the ventricles beat at two thirds of the P wave rate the slider sets, and the RR interval that spans the block is exactly twice the others. The P wave rate of 75 to start with is a model choice. In Mobitz II the QRS is often wide because the block lies below the AV node, in the bundle of His or its branches; the model draws it narrow. Acquired Mobitz II without a reversible or physiological cause is treated with a permanent pacemaker even without symptoms. The model does not show 2:1 or high-grade block, the change to complete block, or the atria contracting on the 3D model.
heartClock.preset.av-block-third-degree-: [RTL] Complete AV block after treatment: pacemaker

[RTL] Rhythm of a dual-chamber pacemaker at {rate} beats per minute. Each beat starts with the heart's own P wave; after a delay comes a narrow vertical pacemaker spike, then a wide QRS complex and a T wave pointing down. The rhythm is regular.

[RTL] Complete AV block without a reversible or physiological cause is treated with a permanent pacemaker, whether or not it causes symptoms. With sinus rhythm the ESC prefers a dual-chamber device to one that paces only the ventricle: it senses the heart's own P wave and, after a set delay, sends an impulse to the ventricles, so the atria and the ventricles work together again. Here every P wave is followed by a narrow vertical spike and a wide QRS complex: the impulse spreads from the lead through the heart muscle, not through the conduction system, and the complex looks like left bundle branch block, where the T wave points the opposite way. The width and shape of the QRS, the T wave, the delay after the P wave and the size of the spike are model choices, since the sources give no numbers for them; on a real ECG the spike can be hard to see. The rate follows the P waves, 75 to start with and 60 to 100 on the slider. The model does not show the pacemaker's lower and upper rate limits or a rate that rises with exercise.
[RTL] Complete AV block: P waves at a steady 75 per minute and, unrelated to them, narrow QRS complexes at {rate} beats per minute. The PR interval keeps changing, and from time to time a P wave falls on a QRS complex or a T wave. Near 37–38 beats per minute the PR changes slowly, and for a while it can look as if every second P wave were conducted.

[RTL] In complete (third-degree) AV block no impulse from the atria reaches the ventricles. The atria keep their own rhythm and the ventricles are driven by a slower escape rhythm, so P waves and QRS complexes are unrelated and the P waves come more often. Here the escape rhythm starts above the branching of the bundle of His: the QRS is narrow and the rate is 35 to 50 beats per minute, 40 to start with. The P waves run at a steady 75 per minute; the sources do not say how regular they are, so this is a model choice. Because the atria and the ventricles no longer work together, the model gives the atria no share in filling the ventricles. The model does not show a slower escape rhythm from the ventricles with a wide QRS (20 to 40 per minute), the large (cannon) a waves in the neck veins, or the atria contracting on the 3D model.
heartClock.preset.brugada-syndrome.ecg: [RTL] Lead V1, sinus rhythm at {rate} beats per minute. Each beat has a P wave, then a QRS complex with a small R wave and a deep S wave. The ST segment starts raised, falls in a dome-shaped (coved) curve and goes into an inverted T wave. The intervals between beats are equal.
heartClock.preset.brugada-syndrome.summa: [RTL] An inherited disorder of the heart's ion channels with a typical ECG and a high risk of ventricular fibrillation and sudden death. The model shows the type 1 pattern in lead V1 only: the J point and the ST segment are raised, and the ST segment is coved and descends into an inverted T wave. The Russian guideline makes the diagnosis when ST elevation of this shape is 2 mm (0.2 mV) or more in V1 or V2; the model raises it by 0.3 mV (3 mm). The rhythm is sinus, and the reader sets the rate. The model draws the raised J point as the start of the ST segment, without the r′-like wave that makes the QRS complex resemble right bundle branch block. It does not show leads V2 and V3, recordings with the electrodes one or two intercostal spaces higher, type 2 and type 3 patterns, how the pattern comes and goes or appears with fever or drugs, or the ventricular arrhythmias that cause fainting and sudden death.
heartClock.preset.heart-failure: [RTL] Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
heartClock.preset.heart-failure.ecg: [RTL] Sinus rhythm at {rate} beats per minute. Each beat has a P wave, then a narrow QRS complex, then a T wave, and the intervals between beats are equal.
heartClock.preset.heart-failure.summary: [RTL] The left ventricle ejects 30% of its volume on each beat instead of about two thirds; a reduced ejection fraction means 40% or less. The ECG does not change, and the model does not play the third heart sound.
heartClock.preset.hypertension.ecg: [RTL] Sinus rhythm at {rate} beats per minute. Each beat has a P wave, then a narrow QRS complex, then a T wave, and the intervals between beats are equal.
heartClock.preset.hypertension.summary: [RTL] Blood pressure is 160/100 mmHg, above the hypertension threshold of 140/90 mmHg; NICE calls this level stage 2. The ECG does not change.
heartClock.preset.long-qt-syndrome.ecg: [RTL] Sinus rhythm at {rate} beats per minute. Each beat has a P wave, then a narrow QRS complex, then a T wave that ends late: the QT interval is long, with a QTc of 500 ms. The intervals between beats are equal.
heartClock.preset.long-qt-syndrome.summa: [RTL] The QT interval is long: the T wave ends later. One of the diagnostic criteria is a QTc of 480 ms or more, and the longer the QTc, especially above 500 ms, the higher the risk of torsades de pointes. The model shows a QTc of 500 ms at every heart rate and does not go above 137 beats per minute: at faster rates a QT this long does not fit between two beats in the model. The model does not show torsades de pointes.
heartClock.preset.normal.ecg: [RTL] Sinus rhythm at {rate} beats per minute. Each beat has a P wave, then a narrow QRS complex, then a T wave, and the intervals between beats are equal.
heartClock.preset.normal.summary: [RTL] Sinus rhythm, pressure in the aorta 120/80 mmHg, and the left ventricle ejects about two thirds of its volume on each beat.
heartClock.preset.sick-sinus-syndrome-pa: [RTL] Sick sinus syndrome after treatment: pacemaker

[RTL] Rhythm of an atrial pacemaker at {rate} beats per minute. Each beat starts with a narrow vertical pacemaker spike, then a P wave, then a narrow QRS complex and a T wave. The rhythm is regular, with no pauses.

[RTL] The main treatment for sick sinus syndrome with symptoms is a permanent pacemaker. The ESC and the Russian guideline recommend a dual-chamber device programmed to avoid pacing the ventricles when it is not needed. The pacemaker sends an impulse when the heart's own rhythm slows down or stops, so the pauses are gone. Here every beat starts with a stimulus to the atria: a narrow vertical spike, then the P wave the stimulus causes, then, when conduction to the ventricles is normal, the usual narrow QRS complex. The model draws the spike larger than it often is: on a real ECG a pacemaker spike can be so small that it is hard to see. The rate is the pacemaker's lower rate, 60 beats per minute to start with and 50 to 70 on the slider; the sources give no single usual setting, so these numbers are a model choice. The model does not show pacing of the ventricles, a rate that rises with exercise, the heart's own beats above the lower rate, or the bouts of fast rhythm of tachy-brady syndrome.
heartClock.preset.sick-sinus-syndrome.ec: [RTL] Sinus bradycardia at {rate} beats per minute. Each beat has a P wave, then a narrow QRS complex, then a T wave. After every third beat there is a pause of 3 seconds with no P wave and no QRS complex: the line stays flat.
heartClock.preset.sick-sinus-syndrome.su: [RTL] The sinus node fires too rarely (sinus bradycardia) and now and then stops (sinus pause). The model keeps the rate below 40 beats per minute: the Russian guideline takes 40 as the lowest normal resting rate by day, and the ESC says 40 to 50 at rest can be normal. The model starts at 35 and keeps the rate from 30 to 39. After every third beat the sinus node is silent for 3 seconds: there is no P wave and no QRS complex, and 4.5 to 5 seconds pass between the beats around the pause. The Russian guideline accepts pauses of up to 2 seconds, and the ESC says pauses longer than 2.5 seconds are rare in healthy people. Real pauses come irregularly, and during a pause lower pacemakers usually take over with escape beats; the model does not draw them. The model does not show tachy-brady syndrome or a heart rate that fails to rise with exercise.
heartClock.preset.stemi.ecg: [RTL] Sinus rhythm at {rate} beats per minute. Each beat has a P wave and a narrow QRS complex; the ST segment after it is raised by 2 mm and runs into the T wave.
heartClock.preset.stemi.summary: [RTL] The ST segment is raised by 2 mm from the J point. A diagnosis needs ST elevation in at least two contiguous leads; the model shows a single lead, similar to lead II, so it shows the inferior wall and no reciprocal changes.
heartClock.preset.supraventricular-tachy: [RTL] Supraventricular tachycardia at {rate} beats per minute. Each beat has a narrow QRS complex with no separate P wave before it, then a T wave, and the intervals between beats are equal.

[RTL] A fast, regular rhythm: in paroxysmal SVT the heart rate is 120 to 250 beats per minute. The model starts at 170 and does not go below 120. The model stops at 180, its upper limit, while the range in the article goes up to 250. The QRS complexes are narrow, and there is no separate P wave: in typical AVNRT the retrograde P′ waves usually merge with the QRS complex. The model does not show the sudden start and end of an episode, or a P′ wave seen at the end of the QRS complex.
heartClock.preset.ventricular-premature-: [RTL] Sinus rhythm at {rate} beats per minute, and every fourth beat comes early. The early beat has no P wave, a wide QRS complex and a T wave pointing the opposite way. After it comes a pause, and the next sinus beat comes when it would have come without the early beat.

[RTL] A premature beat comes earlier than the next normal beat, from an impulse that starts outside the sinus node. In a ventricular premature beat the impulse starts in a ventricle: there is no P wave before it, the QRS is wide, 0.12 s or more, and the T wave points the opposite way. The pause after it is usually fully compensatory. Here every fourth beat is premature, so that the premature beats are easy to see; that is a lot of them, not a typical picture. It comes at 0.7 of the usual interval, and the next sinus beat comes when it would have come without the premature beat, two usual intervals after the beat before it. The QRS width of 140 ms, the depth of the T wave, the timings and that length of the pause are model choices, since the sources give no numbers. The beat before the premature one is cut short, so the model also shortens its contraction; in a real heart the timings of a beat depend on the interval before it, not after it. People usually do not feel the premature beat itself but the stronger beat after it; in the model every beat pumps the same amount. The slider sets the sinus rate from 40 to 86; with this timing the model works only in that range. The model does not show premature beats at random times or in pairs, or where in the ventricles the impulse starts.
heartClock.preset.ventricular-tachycardi: [RTL] Ventricular tachycardia at {rate} beats per minute. Each beat has a wide QRS complex with no P wave before it, then a T wave pointing the opposite way to the QRS complex. The complexes are identical, and the intervals between beats are equal.

[RTL] A fast, regular rhythm that starts in the ventricles: ventricular tachycardia is three or more ventricular beats in a row at more than 100 beats per minute. The model starts at 150 and does not go below 101. The QRS complexes are wide, 120 ms or more, and identical; there is no P wave before them, and the T wave points the opposite way to the main deflection of the QRS complex. The model does not go above 169 beats per minute: at faster rates its wide QRS does not fit the beat. The model does not show AV dissociation (the atria working independently of the ventricles), fusion complexes, polymorphic VT or torsades de pointes, or ventricular fibrillation.
heartClock.preset.wpw-syndrome.ecg: [RTL] Sinus rhythm with pre-excitation at {rate} beats per minute. Each beat has a P wave and, after a short PR interval, a wide QRS complex that starts with a slow rise (the delta wave), then a T wave. The intervals between beats are equal.
heartClock.preset.wpw-syndrome.summary: [RTL] An extra pathway between an atrium and a ventricle bypasses the AV node, so part of the ventricles is activated early (ventricular pre-excitation). Between attacks, in sinus rhythm, the ECG shows a short PR interval, under 120 ms, a slow rise at the start of the QRS complex (the delta wave) and a wide QRS, over 120 ms. In the model PR stays under 120 ms at every rate (about 80 ms at 75 beats per minute), and the QRS is 130 ms, of which the delta wave takes the first 40 ms. The model does not go above 153 beats per minute: at faster rates its late R peak does not fit the beat. In the model the P wave shortens along with PR; on a real ECG the P wave keeps its usual length. WPW syndrome means pre-excitation together with recurring attacks of tachycardia; the model shows only the ECG between attacks. It does not show the tachycardias themselves (orthodromic or antidromic AV reentrant tachycardia), atrial fibrillation conducted over the extra pathway, the secondary changes of the ST segment and T wave, other leads, or the extra pathway in the 3D model.
heartClock.schematic: [RTL] A schematic teaching model, not a recording and not for diagnosis. Not reviewed by a physician. Durations follow published averages and are simplified; some values are model assumptions.
heartClock.title: [RTL] Heart clock
heartClock.wiggers.description: [RTL] During ventricular systole the pressure in the left ventricle rises above the aortic pressure and blood is ejected, so the ventricular volume falls. After the aortic valve closes the pressure in the ventricle drops below the atrial pressure, the mitral valve opens and the ventricle fills again; atrial contraction adds the last part of the filling.
heartClock.wiggers.label: [RTL] Wiggers diagram: pressure in the left ventricle, aorta and left atrium, left ventricular volume and the ECG over one cardiac cycle, with a cursor at the current moment.
heartClock.wiggers.title: [RTL] Wiggers diagram
heartSounds.intro: [RTL] A doctor listens to the heart with a stethoscope: two heart sounds in every beat and, with a valve disease, a murmur between or after them. Pick a sound and press Listen. It plays in step with the heart clock at 60 beats per minute, and the diagram shows where in the cycle each sound falls.
heartSounds.link: [RTL] Listen to heart sounds and valve murmurs
heartSounds.schematic: [RTL] The sounds are synthesised from descriptions in medical references. This is a teaching model, not a patient recording and not a diagnostic tool. Pitches are higher than real heart sounds so phone speakers can play them. Not reviewed by a physician.
heartSounds.sound.aortic-regurgitation.d: [RTL] A diastolic murmur that starts soon after the second sound and fades away (decrescendo). It is high-pitched and blowing. It is loudest at the third or fourth intercostal space left of the sternum or at the apex, and is heard best with the person leaning forward and holding their breath after breathing out. When the regurgitation is slight, the murmur may be heard only in early diastole.
heartSounds.sound.aortic-stenosis.descri: [RTL] An ejection murmur in mid-systole: it starts after the first sound, rises and falls (crescendo-decrescendo) and ends before the second sound. It sounds harsh or grating. It is heard best at the right and left upper sternal border, with the person sitting up and leaning forward, and spreads to the right collarbone and both carotid arteries. The second sound is soft or single. As the stenosis gets more severe, the murmur gets longer and peaks later in systole; the player shows a moderate one.
heartSounds.sound.mitral-regurgitation.d: [RTL] A holosystolic (pansystolic) murmur: it fills all of systole, from the first to the second sound, at the same loudness. It is heard best at the apex, with the person lying on their left side, and spreads to the left armpit. The first sound is soft.
heartSounds.sound.mitral-stenosis.descri: [RTL] A loud first sound. Soon after the second sound (0.06–0.11 s) comes the opening snap (OS) of the mitral valve, then a low-pitched rumbling diastolic murmur: it fades, then grows again just before the next first sound, when the atria contract. It is heard at the apex of the heart, best with the person lying on their left side, and does not spread anywhere. With atrial fibrillation the presystolic rise disappears.
[RTL] A high-pitched click in mid-systole: the structures under the valve (the chordae tendineae) suddenly tighten as the leaflet prolapses. If blood leaks back through the valve (regurgitation), a late systolic murmur follows the click, as in the player. Prolapse without regurgitation often gives only the click. It is heard best at the apex, with the person lying on their left side.
heartSounds.sound.normal.description: [RTL] Two short sounds in every beat. The first (S1) comes at the start of ventricular systole, mostly from the mitral valve closing. The second (S2) comes at the start of diastole, when the aortic and pulmonary valves close. Together they make the familiar “lub-dub”.

viewer.disease.aortic-stenosis.beat: [RTL] The aortic valve does not open fully: the opening is narrowed.
viewer.disease.atrial-fibrillation.beat: [RTL] The atria do not contract effectively, so on the model they do not squeeze.
viewer.disease.atrial-septal-defect: [RTL] The marker shows where the hole in the wall between the atria is. The model does not show the hole itself.
viewer.disease.coronary-heart-disease: [RTL] An example: a heart attack in the lower (inferior) wall of the left ventricle. The area usually supplied by the right coronary artery is coloured darker.
viewer.disease.coronary-heart-disease.be: [RTL] While the heart beats, the coloured area moves less than the rest of the wall.
viewer.disease.heart-failure.beat: [RTL] Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction: the ventricles contract less than normal.
viewer.disease.hypertension: [RTL] The left ventricle is highlighted: in high blood pressure its wall can thicken (hypertrophy). The model does not show wall thickness.
viewer.disease.hypertrophic-cardiomyopat: [RTL] The left ventricle is highlighted, and its part next to the septum is darker. In HCM the left ventricular wall in adults is 15 mm or thicker in at least one part, often unevenly because of the septum. The model does not show wall thickness.
viewer.disease.note: [RTL] The signs of disease are a schematic: sizes and colours are chosen to be easy to see.
viewer.error: [RTL] The 3D model could not be loaded. The list of structures still works.
viewer.heartbeat.note: [RTL] The heartbeat is a schematic: the atria and then the ventricles contract and the valves open in time with a model of the cardiac cycle, but the size of the movement is exaggerated so it is easy to see.
viewer.keyboardHelp: [RTL] Drag to rotate. Click the model, then scroll or pinch to zoom. With the keyboard, focus the model, then use the arrow keys to rotate, + and − to zoom, and 0 or Home to reset the view.

viewer.schematic: [RTL] The conduction system is a schematic drawing: its position is approximate, placed after a published anatomical description rather than taken from the source model.
viewer.unavailable: [RTL] This browser cannot show 3D graphics (WebGL). The picture and the list of structures still work.
